question: How does blood move through the heart?
answer: Blood follows a set path through the heart's two sides. Oxygen-poor blood coming back from the body enters the right side, made up of the right atrium and right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. In the lungs the blood picks up fresh oxygen and turns red. This oxygen-rich blood then enters the left side, the left atrium and left ventricle, which pumps it out through the aorta to supply the body's tissues. Four valves (tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic) act like one-way gates so blood only flows in the right direction. Each heartbeat has two phases. In systole the ventricles contract and squeeze blood into the vessels leading to the lungs and body, with the right ventricle contracting slightly before the left. In diastole the ventricles relax and refill with blood from the atria above them. Electrical impulses that start high in the right atrium keep this cycle beating in a coordinated rhythm.
